job.style: a passage that starts from a common wrong idea and corrects it

passage: Many people believe that if a caller knows their name or claims to be from a bank, they are trustworthy and must follow instructions immediately to avoid account closure. This is a dangerous myth. Banks will never ask you to share your OTP, PIN, or CVV over a phone call, even if they claim it is for a KYC update. If you receive a message asking you to click a link to update your KYC, do not click it, as legitimate banks do not operate this way. Furthermore, some scammers promise high monthly returns on investments and ask you to keep the deal secret from your family. They might even show you a fancy office or a certificate to look official. Remember, a high-return scheme that requires secrecy is almost always a fraud. If you ever lose money, do not wait or feel ashamed; report the incident immediately to the official cybercrime portal or your bank. Never trust a phone number provided by a stranger; always use the official contact details found on the back of your debit card or the bank's verified website. By staying alert and never sharing your secret banking codes, you can keep your money safe from those who try to trick you.

items.evidence: Banks will never ask you to share your OTP, PIN, or CVV over a phone call, even if they claim it is for a KYC update.
items.q: A caller who knows your name asks for your OTP. What does this most likely show?
options: He is most likely a cheat
He is a real bank worker
He is genuine, as he knows you
He is warning you of account closure
items.explain: Banks never ask for OTPs on calls, so a caller asking for one is probably a scammer.

wrong.why: thinks sharing an OTP with a bank employee is fine
thinks knowing your name proves the caller is genuine
believes the account will close immediately

items.evidence: If you receive a message asking you to click a link to update your KYC, do not click it, as legitimate banks do not operate this way.
items.q: An SMS asks you to update KYC through a link. What is the safest step?
options: Ignore it and contact the bank yourself
Reply to it to check if it is real
Open it fast before the account closes
Tap it, since a link alone is harmless
items.explain: Legitimate banks do not ask for KYC updates through links, so do not click; contact the bank directly.

wrong.why: thinks replying just to check is harmless
fears the account closes within hours
thinks a link only harms if you enter details

items.evidence: Remember, a high-return scheme that requires secrecy is almost always a fraud.
items.q: A man promises big monthly profit and asks you to hide the deal from family. What does this hint?
options: It hints at a trap to cheat you
It keeps your special chance safe
It shows he runs his business well
It is normal for high-return deals
items.explain: A high-return scheme that demands secrecy is almost always a fraud, so the secrecy is a warning sign.

wrong.why: thinks secrecy only protects a special chance
thinks very high returns show business skill
over-generalises that secrecy is normal in such deals

items.evidence: They might even show you a fancy office or a certificate to look official.
items.q: A scheme shows you a fancy office and a certificate. What should you conclude?
options: The papers and office prove nothing
The office proves the scheme is genuine
The certificate makes high returns guaranteed
The scheme is safe to share with friends
items.explain: Scammers use fancy offices and certificates to look official, so these do not prove a scheme is safe.

wrong.why: thinks a written guarantee makes a scheme safe
thinks bringing friends in is safe because everyone gains

items.evidence: Never trust a phone number provided by a stranger; always use the official contact details found on the back of your debit card or the bank's verified website.
items.q: Where can you safely find your bank's real contact number?
options: From your debit card or verified website
From a normal-looking 10-digit mobile number
From the caller who says he is from the bank
From the SMS that asks for your KYC
items.explain: Use the contact details on the back of your debit card or the bank's verified website.

wrong.why: thinks a normal-looking mobile number is safe
trusts a caller who claims to be from the bank
trusts the KYC message and its instructions
